title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Pool and spa servicing
audience: Owners of small Australian pool and spa servicing businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short visits, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A pool rate depends on chemistry skill, the equipment the business carries, the mix of visits and repairs, whether the work is licensed in the state where it is done, and how many pools sit on the same route. A round of nearby fortnightly accounts is cheaper to run than scattered one-off jobs, and that should show in the rate. Local evidence is patchy. A Melbourne vendor cost guide gives fortnightly service at $135 to $315 a month, typically about $220, with chemicals extra. It also gives a chemistry-only visit at $84 to $190 and a one-off clean at $105 to $370 (What's The Damage?, updated November 2026). That is one vendor's figure for one city, so use it as a check, not a target. An Airtasker page on pool cleaning (last updated 17 January 2023) gives per-job ranges, but its introduction gives a different range from its table, so use it only as a rough check.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel between pools, quoting, admin, marketing, training, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract the non-billable time to reach billable hours. Jobber's general guidance puts billable time at about 60 to 80 percent of working hours, but that is a general range and not an Australian figure, so check your own log against it. A route of pools close together raises the billable share. A day of long drives between pools lowers it.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, registration, test kits and equipment upkeep, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income needed to live on. Business.gov.au says on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure, so decide how each will be allowed for, and have a registered tax agent confirm the treatment for your own situation before you publish the rate (1 October 2026). Xero Australia works the same way: take-home pay, business costs and super are added together and divided by billable hours. Its own example gives about $81 an hour, from 25 billable hours in a 38-hour week, and that example is not a pool rate. Review the base rate each quarter, and compare it with what clients accept.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short visits
instruction.body: A chemistry-only visit can cost more in travel and set-up time than it earns, because the drive to the pool and the test set-up do not shrink with the size of the task. A minimum charge or a call-out fee covers the time needed to attend the site. Set the minimum so that a short visit still covers travel, set-up, the test and admin. Contractor+ suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, dividing that cost by one minus the target margin. Its example is labelled illustrative by the source: a $105 visit cost at a 30 percent target margin gives a $150 minimum. Do not stack a separate minimum on each task. Price several small tasks at one visit as one labour amount, and price any extra work before you start it. State the minimum before the visit and explain it in plain words.

instruction.heading: Review and raise the rate
instruction.body: Business Victoria recommends reviewing prices about every three months, and checking that they still suit the business and its customers (undated page). Raise the rate when your costs rise, not only once a year. Give existing clients written notice of any change, and honour quotes that were already approved at the old rate.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, test kits, equipment, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by the billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin for a short visit, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: An owner's calculation shows that only sixty of every hundred paid hours can be billed (illustrative), because the rest go on driving between pools and on admin. The owner plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate if the wrong assumption is kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: Pricing as if every paid hour were billable understates the rate, because the costs and the income still have to come out of the hours that can be billed. At a 60 per cent billable share (illustrative), the rate must be about 1.67 times the rate needed for a fully billable week (1 divided by 0.6). The rate must be built from billable hours, then checked against the local evidence and the minimum charge before it is published.

equipmentAndPpe: Log of paid and billable hours for one month, with the drive time between pools marked separately
Price sheet with the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a vendor's figure or a competitor's price without checking your own costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed, including the drive between pools.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time, including travel, before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking a short chemistry visit at the same rate, without covering travel and set-up.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited (setting prices: what's allowed, 15 July 2026). The ACCC guidance cited here does not settle minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term, so check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.

Licence scope limits what you can price. In Queensland, the QBCC swimming pool construction, installation and maintenance class covers maintenance and general repair. Plumbing, drainage, gasfitting and termite work need separate licences (QBCC trade class page, dated 31 August 2021, check the current scope). Do not include licensed work in a rate unless you hold the licence that covers it in that state.
Confirm the tax treatment of leave, superannuation and the owner's own income with a registered tax agent before publishing the rate.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short visit.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short visits.

knowledgeChecks.question: A pool owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per visit
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for short pool visits?
options: Because short visits need travel but no set-up time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, set-up and admin time does not shrink with the size of the visit
Because clients expect every visit to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate for a pool business?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure; going-rate pricing.

Xero Australia, 'How to price services', https://www.xero.com/au/guides/how-to-price-services/, dated 3 September 2026. Supports: rate from take-home pay, business costs and super divided by billable hours. The page's example is not a pool rate.

Jobber, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. General range, not an Australian figure. Supports: billable time typically 60 to 80 percent of working hours.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, 23 September 2026. The source labels its figures illustrative, not market rates. Supports: minimum set from the full visit cost divided by one minus target margin; the minimum covers travel, set-up and admin.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: review prices about every three months.

What's The Damage?, 'Weekly vs monthly pool service cost in Melbourne', https://whatsthedamage.com.au/pool-maintenance-cost-melbourne/weekly-vs-monthly-service-cost/, marked updated November 2026, prices verified 1 November 2026. Vendor source (lead generation). Supports: fortnightly service $135 to $315 a month; chemistry-only visit $84 to $190; one-off clean $105 to $370.

Airtasker, 'Pool cleaning cost', https://www.airtasker.com/pool-maintenance/pool-cleaning/price/pool-cleaning-cost/, last updated 17 January 2023. Marketplace source. Its introduction and its table give different ranges, so it is used only as a rough check.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.

QBCC, 'Swimming pool construction, installation and maintenance', https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/licences/apply-licence/available-licences/other-trade/swimming-pool-construction-installation, page dated 31 August 2021. Queensland. Supports: the trade class covers maintenance and general repair; plumbing, drainage, gasfitting and termite work need separate licences.

Gap: no pool minimum or call-out charge from a trade or government source was opened. No Australian pool trade-body source (for example SPASA) was reached. Minimum-charge rules for Australian pool work were not confirmed.
